en: Homage to Mañjuśrī, the Refuter of Birth.
He who sprinkles with the saffron-red water of his own splendor, poured forth from the golden jars of his feet whose tender sprouts are his lovely fingers,
upon one who salutes him, establishing him in the kingdom of Dharma.
May that Mañjunātha remain awake for the sake of our welfare and happiness.
Out of consideration for my friends, and according to my own understanding and memory,
I shall set down here some points of debate, casting aside all sense of shame.
In this regard, first of all, the doctrine of genus (*jāti*) is refuted.
Here, whatever cannot be designated as either different from or identical to a thing is not that thing;
for example, a sky-lotus.
Furthermore, a universal is not denotable by way of either difference or non-difference from a real entity;
this is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
First of all, this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Indeed, it is impossible to designate a universal as either distinct from or non-distinct from individuals;
for in either case, the consequence follows that it would lack the very nature of being a universal.
To explain: if, first of all, the entity regarded as the universal were indeed a different object from the individuals, then how could it be called their "universal"?
Indeed, that which is a different entity from something cannot be its universal;
for example, a horse is not the universal of a cow. And "cowness" is a different entity from a cow.
[This is] the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory. Now, one might object: "How can the universal be both distinct from the individuals and yet belong to them?
We see no contradiction here.
Nor should it be thought that if one thing were the universal of another thing, then everything would be the universal of everything due to the absence of distinction; for indeed,
that entity which inheres in many things is the universal belonging to them.
Since a horse is not included among cows, how could it be the commonality (*sāmānya*) of cows? Thus, how can there be an absence of distinction?
Consequently, this reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); how could it suffice to establish the desired conclusion?
Therefore, this too merely resembles the prattle of a child.
For that specific distinction must be stated by the intelligent one, which—while existing solely in the entity accepted as a universal—would establish a non-confused determination.
And since this inherence in multiple things exists even in number, conjunction, the body, substance, and so forth, these too would be universals according to the Sāṃkhya and other schools.
Now, you might think as follows:
Even though there is a co-inherence of many objects, that alone is the universal (*sāmānya*) which serves as the basis for the occurrence of identical cognition and designation, and nothing else.
For a universal is the state (*bhāva*) of those things that are similar.
It is called "state" (*bhāva*) because from it arise both the designation and the cognition.
Regarding this, he says:
"The universal (*jāti*) consists in the production of identical cognitions and designations.
This too is merely an illumination of one's own [unorthodox] system.
For in this case, two alternatives arise:
are they identical in their own nature, or is it that a universal (*sāmānya*) has arisen among those produced from such causes, which is inclined toward such cognition and verbal designation?

Or rather, are they simply identical? In that case, if they are identical by their very nature, then in the process of cognition and designation, they will function as nothing other than [the object] itself.
What is the use of a separate entity as a universal (sāmānya) in that case?
For it would simply not be a universal,
since by its power, identical cognition and designation would fail to occur.
If they are not similar, then there is no commonality among them, for you have stated that "the state of being similar is commonality. And yet,
the "Beloved of the Gods," whose wisdom is truly praiseworthy, asserts that "the state of being dissimilar is commonality."
If it is argued that although they are by nature dissimilar, they are nevertheless not [truly] dissimilar,
then what is being done to them? Are they being produced, or are they being conceptually determined (*adhyavasīyante*)?
In that regard, they are not produced [anew],
because they have already been produced by their own causes,
and because it is impossible to produce again what has already been produced.

If it is argued that because the instrument (*karaṇa*) has the characteristic of being a manifestation of what was previously non-existent, [the objects] are "made" (*kriyante*) by means of a common essence;
[we reply: surely, for those things whose status as the object (*karman*) of the root *kṛ* does not exist due to their already being accomplished (*niṣpanna*), how can they be said to be "made"?
It might be so: in the form of a substrate (*dharmin*) in which they are accomplished, they do not undergo the state of being the object of the verb *kṛ*.
Furthermore, since they are produced by that very same identical form (*samāna-rūpa*), there is nothing here that is logically inconsistent.

If that were so, one might argue that it is that very same identical form which is produced through a universal (*sāmānya*); yet, regarding its existence, it would be impossible even for Brahmā to establish that something which is unproduced and arises later from another cause possesses the nature of that [universal].
If it is argued that let it be a different entity altogether and nothing undesirable follows,
then it must be a different universal; thus, the birth of a non-universal would have been accepted.

And likewise, when it is further questioned how that [universal] can be a commonality for particulars that are themselves dissimilar, if one resorts to the assumption that it too produces a similar form distinct from those particulars, then an infinite regress—consisting of the postulation of ever-further universals of action—is incurred, which cannot be avoided; nor does the dissimilarity of the particulars thereby disappear. Furthermore, resorting to the second alternative is not preferable.
For it is not the case that things are perceived as being "identical" through something other than themselves; rather, they would be perceived as possessing that [quality].
It is like the quality [of roughness] in the throat, which exists as a real entity (*bhūta*).
Otherwise, anything whatsoever might be perceived as identical with anything else, because there would be no basis for restriction.

If it is argued that there is no over-extension because things are perceived as identical through one [universal] inhering in many, while other things are perceived as identical through another [universal],
this is trivial; for it is not the case that the parts of a whole, substances, duality, and so forth, lack the state of having both unity and multiple [universals] inhering in them.
Otherwise, parts (*avayava*) and the like would not be understood from them.

Now, if it is argued that there is no fault because those [universals] lack the capacity for identical cognition and designation in relation to their own substrates, [we reply: surely the universal (*sāmānya*) also serves as the cause of identical cognition toward its particulars (*bheda*) precisely through both oneness and manifold inherence (*samavāya*). Since you yourselves accept these two [oneness and manifold inherence] even for the composite whole (*avayavin*) and so forth, how can their status as such be avoided?

If it is argued that because they lack a common nature (*asāmānya-svabhāvatva*), they are not causes for a uniform cognition (*samāna-jñāna*), then [we reply]: surely, the absence of a common nature exists only when there is no causality for a uniform cognition; and if that [absence of a common nature] exists, there is no causality for a uniform cognition. Thus, a clear case of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is evident.

For instance, when you were asked why substance (*dravya*) and so forth should not also possess the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*), given that they share the same status as oneness (*ekatva*) and other such properties which are accepted as universals, you replied that it is because [substance] does not produce a cognition of similarity (*samānapratyaya*).

Yet, when we in turn ask why the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth should not also be similar—since the cause of the cognition of similarity is itself similar—you respond by saying that it is because [the whole] lacks the nature of a universal; however, one who says this cannot consistently maintain that [oneness] is a single entity.
And having directly asserted its oneness and eternity, he then contradicts that very point through another teaching; how, then, is he not insane?
Therefore, it is established that the universal exists through both difference and non-difference.
But surely this reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

For although a universal (*sāmānya*) is not denotable by either difference or non-difference alone, nevertheless it is not a non-entity (*avastu*), because there is the possibility of another mode characterized by both natures; indeed, the Jains and the followers of Jaimini maintain that the universal is both different and non-different. As they say:
One who seeks a pot, a crown, or gold undergoes grief, joy, or indifference—each with its respective cause—upon the destruction, production, or persistence [of these objects]. (1)
It does not arise nor does it perish in its general nature, because its continuity is manifest;
yet it perishes and arises through its particularity, for existence involves arising and so forth within a single locus.
Just as one who possesses a variegated color can assume whatever form is desired, so too, because an object is manifold, there is the determination of both difference and non-difference. (3)
But when a variegated object is perceived simultaneously, then every distinction such as identity and difference is cognized. (4)
"That which is of a single nature must be one" is not the teaching of the Lord;
for it should be accepted exactly as it is perceived. (5) Thus.
To this, it is replied:

Since difference and non-difference are of the nature of mutual exclusion, and since the affirmation of one is inseparable from the negation of the other, how could anyone other than a drunkard or a madman maintain that these two reside in a single substratum?
To explain:
That which is non-different from something is indeed identical to it;
and that which is different from something is not that thing.

Therefore, one who asserts that the universal is both different and non-different from the individuals is effectively saying that the individuals are the universal, yet the individuals are not the universal.
And how could one with a sound mind superimpose this upon that?
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever is thus [as it appears] does not become otherwise, just as the nature of fire, which is hot, is not non-hot.
To claim that individuals alone are the universal would entail the undesirable consequence of perceiving what is contradictory to their own nature.
If it is argued that both are accepted because both are perceived, we reply:
indeed, perception sublates non-perception, but it does not sublate a false perception.
Because even that which is false is seen to be perceived;
for otherwise, if you— who follow perception as it appears— were to deny things such as a double moon on account of their falsity,
why does the "Beloved of the Gods" not see here as well this inference produced from a logical mark (liṅga) that is free from the three defects, such as being unestablished?

If it is argued that consciousness is not sublated by reasonings, is this perhaps a royal decree by which consciousness—being direct perception in its very nature—is to be accepted without investigation? And if it is further argued that because it is the foremost means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it cannot be sublated; [we reply: no.

In that case, that inference would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If sublation were impossible for that which possesses the defining characteristics [of a valid cognition], then those very characteristics would be undermined, resulting in a lack of confidence in all cases.
Just as a fallacious inference is sublated, why should a fallacious perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) not also be sublated?
If it is argued that while the pseudo-perception (pratyakṣābhāsa) may be sublated, this consciousness is indeed a direct perception (pratyakṣa), and therefore how can it not be unsublatable?
[We reply: But even this is a pseudo-perception, because it is sublated by inference (anumāna).
Now, if there is the insistence that perception alone establishes the fallacious nature of another perception because it is sublated, and not inference,
then how is the status of recognition regarding a flame or the like established as a fallacy of perception with respect to the individual [object]?
For indeed, perception would not determine the non-momentariness of flames and such things.

Therefore, inference alone must establish the momentariness of flames and the like; even an unwilling Kumārila must admit that this [perception] is sublated by it. It cannot be argued that only the universal (*sāmānya*) is made its object by that [perception], for if that were the case, the cognition would be "this is flame-ness," rather than "this is that very same flame."
Therefore, the reason is not inconclusive; enough with this excessive talk.
This is the refutation of caste by the venerable Jitāri.
